schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
counterexample: INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (1, 1, 2); INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (2, 1, 1); INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (1, 3, 1);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 uses a subquery with IN to match (X.EMP, X.DEPT) against (Y.MGR, Y.DEPT) from DEPT where LOC = 3. Q2 uses an explicit join between EMP and DEPT on DEPT and matches X.EMP = Y.MGR and Y.LOC = 3. These are logically different conditions, leading to different results in some cases.
counterexample_dsp: A case where an employee (X) has the same DEPT as a department (Y), but X.EMP does not equal Y.MGR, and another employee matches both X.EMP = Y.MGR and Y.LOC = 3. This will cause Q1 to return more rows than Q2.
